content: Tap the person's shoulder firmly and shout 'Are you okay?' If there is no response or only groaning, treat them as unresponsive. Do not delay activating emergency services.
Look at the chest for no more than 10 seconds. Normal breathing is regular and you can clearly see chest rise. Agonal gasping is NOT normal breathing — start CPR if gasping or not breathing.
Call 911 immediately or direct a specific bystander to call. Put the phone on speaker. Send someone to retrieve an AED if one is nearby. Do not leave the person alone unless absolutely necessary.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest on the lower half of the sternum. Place the other hand on top, interlace fingers. Keep fingers off the ribs and off the upper abdomen.
Deliver compressions at 100 to 120 per minute. A rate near 110 per minute is ideal. Use a metronome app or mentally count to 'Stayin' Alive' rhythm. Minimize pauses between compressions.
For adults, compress at least 5 cm (2 inches) and no more than 6 cm (2.4 inches). Inadequate depth is the most common CPR error. Push hard enough to depress the chest fully.
Allow complete chest recoil after every compression. Do not lean on the chest. Incomplete recoil reduces blood flow and is a common performance error during CPR.
Kneel beside the person. Keep your shoulders directly over your hands. Lock your elbows and use your body weight to compress straight down. Avoid rocking or angled force.
Start CPR immediately if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. For bystanders, do not spend more than 10 seconds checking for a pulse before starting compressions.
If you are unwilling or unable to give rescue breaths, perform continuous chest compressions. Compression-only CPR is effective for adult sudden cardiac arrest in the first minutes.
Turn on the AED and follow voice prompts. Apply pads as shown on the diagram. Ensure nobody touches the person during shock analysis or delivery. Resume CPR immediately after a shock.
Switch compressors every 2 minutes or sooner if you become fatigued. Fatigue causes shallow compressions within 1-2 minutes. Minimize interruption time during the switch.

For infants under 1 year: use two fingers or two-thumb encircling technique on the center of the chest. Compress about 4 cm deep at 100-120 per minute. Cover the infant's mouth and nose for breaths if trained.
For children: compress with one or two hands depending on size. Depth about 5 cm. Same rate of 100-120 per minute. After 5 cycles, call 911 if you were alone.
If the person becomes responsive and is breathing normally, place them in the recovery position. Monitor breathing continuously until EMS arrives.
For unresponsive choking: start CPR and look in the mouth for visible object before breaths. Do not blind finger sweeps. Use standard choking response steps for responsive victims separately.
Ensure the scene is safe for you and the victim before approaching. Use personal protective equipment if available. Move the person only if the environment is immediately dangerous.
High-quality CPR requires: rate 100-120, depth 5-6 cm, full recoil, minimal interruptions, and correct hand placement on the lower sternum. These five metrics predict survival.
Every pause in compressions reduces coronary perfusion pressure. Pre-charge AED during compressions when possible. Limit interruption to less than 10 seconds for any reason including breaths or AED.
Bystander CPR doubles or triples survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. You cannot make the person worse — doing something is better than doing nothing. Any attempt is valuable.
